title: GOD SAID HIS PEOPLE WERE WORSE THAN AN UNFAITHFUL WIFE—BECAUSE THEY WERE PAYING THE VERY LOVERS WHO BETRAYED THEM.
paragraphs: GOD SAID HIS PEOPLE WERE WORSE THAN AN UNFAITHFUL WIFE—BECAUSE THEY WERE PAYING THE VERY LOVERS WHO BETRAYED THEM.

One of the most disturbing accusations in the Bible reveals a terrifying truth about sin, the heartbreak of spiritual unfaithfulness, and the astonishing grace of a Savior who still calls sinners home.
“How weak is thine heart, saith the Lord GOD, seeing thou doest all these things, the work of an imperious whorish woman.” — Ezekiel 16:30 (KJV)
There are things God said in Scripture that are so uncomfortable, so devastating, and so painfully honest that we would rather skip the passage than allow it to examine us.
Ezekiel 16 is one of them.
Because in this chapter, God does not merely accuse His people of breaking a rule.
He describes them as an unfaithful wife.
But then He says something even more shocking.
She was not simply running after other lovers.
She was paying them to take the place of the One who had already loved her.
Read that again.
She was giving away what her faithful Husband had provided, spending His gifts to pursue the very relationships that were destroying her.
And before we shake our heads at ancient Jerusalem, we need to confront an uncomfortable possibility.
What if we have been doing something remarkably similar?
What if the very breath God gave us has been used to ignore Him?
What if the money He entrusted to us has been spent nurturing the idols that pull our hearts away from Him?
What if the time He gave us to live has been consumed by everything except the One who gives life?
What if we have been asking God to bless the very things that are slowly replacing Him?
And what if the greatest tragedy is not simply that we have wandered away...
But that we have become so comfortable in our wandering that we no longer recognize how far we have gone?
Stay with this passage.
Because the God who exposes the scandal of unfaithfulness is also the God who reveals a grace that no unfaithful sinner could ever deserve.
And the ending is far more beautiful than the beginning.
Before God confronted Jerusalem's betrayal, He reminded her of something she had forgotten.
He reminded her where she came from.
In Ezekiel 16, Jerusalem is portrayed as an abandoned newborn, unwanted, neglected, and left helpless.
No one cared enough to rescue her.
No one had washed her.
No one had wrapped her.
No one had shown her compassion.
Then God passed by.
And in one of the most extraordinary declarations of divine mercy in the Old Testament, He said:

“And when I passed by thee, and saw thee polluted in thine own blood, I said unto thee when thou wast in thy blood, Live; yea, I said unto thee when thou wast in thy blood, Live.” — Ezekiel 16:6 (KJV)
Live.
One word.
Spoken over a life that had been left to die.
She had done nothing to deserve His attention.
She had achieved nothing to earn His affection.
She had no beauty, wealth, reputation, or accomplishments to offer Him.
Yet He chose to give her life.
That is where the story begins.
Not with human goodness.
Not with religious achievement.
Not with a sinner climbing high enough to reach God.
It begins with mercy.
God came to someone who could not rescue herself.
And He said, "Live."
Maybe that is why this passage is so personal.
Because some of us remember what life looked like before the Lord began changing us.
We remember the emptiness we tried to hide.
The nights when we cried without telling anyone.
The guilt we carried.
The destructive decisions.
The relationships we thought would heal us but only wounded us more deeply.
The moments when we wondered whether anything good could ever come from our lives.
And somewhere in that darkness, the mercy of God reached us.
Not because we were impressive.
But because He is merciful.
Yet Jerusalem eventually forgot the One who had rescued her.
God clothed her, adorned her, provided for her, and entered into a covenant relationship with her.
She became beautiful through what He had given.
And then something heartbreaking happened.
She began trusting in the beauty God had given her instead of trusting in the God who had made her beautiful.
Ezekiel 16:15 says:
“But thou didst trust in thine own beauty, and playedst the harlot because of thy renown...”
There it is.
The turning point.
The gift became more important than the Giver.
The blessing became a substitute for the One who blessed.
And the heart that had once depended entirely upon God began imagining it could flourish without Him.
Does that sound familiar?
Sometimes the most dangerous moment in our spiritual lives is not when we have nothing.
It is when we finally have something.
When the prayers have been answered.
When the bills are paid.
When the relationship begins.
When the business grows.
When the opportunities arrive.
When people start noticing us.
When life becomes comfortable enough that our desperation for God slowly disappears.
We prayed for the blessing.
Then we became too busy enjoying the blessing to spend time with the One who gave it.
We begged God to open a door.
Then walked through it and stopped seeking His direction.
We asked Him to heal our hearts.
Then handed those hearts to something that could never love us as He does.
Not every blessing becomes an idol.
But anything good can become spiritually dangerous when we give it the devotion that belongs to God alone.
And that brings us to one of the most disturbing accusations in Ezekiel.
God says:
“But as a wife that committeth adultery, which taketh strangers instead of her husband!” — Ezekiel 16:32 (KJV)
Then comes the shocking reversal:
“They give gifts to all whores: but thou givest thy gifts to all thy lovers, and hirest them, that they may come unto thee on every side for thy whoredom.” — Ezekiel 16:33 (KJV)
In the ordinary pattern described by the prophet, the prostitute receives payment.
But Jerusalem's spiritual unfaithfulness was portrayed as so extreme that she reversed the arrangement.
She paid those she pursued.
She used what she possessed to attract the very lovers who represented her betrayal.
And God was not describing a minor personal weakness.
He was exposing covenant unfaithfulness.
The Hebrew text makes the accusation especially striking.
In Ezekiel 16:30, the phrase מָה אֲמֻלָּה לִבָּתֵךְ (mah amullah libbatekh) expresses God's accusation concerning the condition of Jerusalem's heart.
The opening word, mah, introduces an exclamation.
The phrase concerns how weak or sick her heart has become, depending on how the Hebrew is understood and translated.
The King James Version renders it, “How weak is thine heart.”
The language is not simply about a moment of sadness.
It belongs to a divine indictment of a people whose desires, decisions, and covenant loyalties had become profoundly corrupted.
Then in verse 33, the Hebrew uses שֹׁחַד (shochad), a word associated with a gift or bribe.
The imagery is devastating.
Jerusalem was not merely being seduced.
She was actively using her resources to pursue her false lovers.
And in verse 34, God emphasizes the reversal: unlike the usual arrangement, she was giving payment rather than receiving it.
The Hebrew intensifies what the English translations already make clear.
God's people had become so committed to their unfaithfulness that they were financing it themselves.
But we must understand the passage correctly.

Ezekiel 16 is a prophetic allegory directed toward Jerusalem, representing the covenant unfaithfulness of God's people. Its marriage imagery is not permission to humiliate women, blame victims of sexual abuse, or treat every human relationship failure as equivalent to idolatry.
The chapter condemns Jerusalem's idolatry and moral corruption, including grievous injustice and the sacrifice of children.
God is exposing the betrayal of a covenant relationship that He Himself had established.
And the accusation becomes even more serious when we remember what those false lovers represented.
They were not merely romantic competitors.
They represented false gods, corrupt alliances, misplaced trust, and spiritual rebellion.
Jerusalem had turned from the Lord toward powers and practices that could not save her.
And she used the very gifts God had provided to sustain that rebellion.
Now bring that truth into the present.
Because an idol does not always look like a carved statue.
Sometimes it looks like approval.
Sometimes it looks like money.
Sometimes it looks like a relationship we refuse to surrender.
Sometimes it looks like an addiction we secretly protect.
Sometimes it looks like a reputation we will compromise anything to maintain.
Sometimes it looks like a screen we cannot put down long enough to pray.
Sometimes it looks like success.
Sometimes it even looks like religious activity.
We can become so devoted to being admired for serving God that we stop caring whether we are actually walking with Him.
We can know the language of worship while our hearts are occupied by other masters.
We can post Scripture publicly while privately refusing to obey what Scripture says.
We can sing about surrender on Sunday and spend the rest of the week negotiating which parts of our lives Jesus is allowed to touch.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that none of this requires us to announce that we have abandoned God.
We can drift while still calling ourselves believers.
We can compromise while still attending church.
We can grow spiritually cold while still knowing exactly how to sound spiritually alive.
That is why this passage should not simply make us angry at Jerusalem.
It should make us examine ourselves.
Because there is a question buried beneath the prophetic accusation.
What have I been giving my heart to that cannot give me life in return?
Think about that carefully.
How much peace have you surrendered trying to impress people who barely know you?
How much time have you spent chasing things that leave you emptier when you finally obtain them?
How many convictions have you silenced because obedience threatened something you did not want to lose?
How many times have you felt the Spirit's conviction through the truth of Scripture and responded, "Later, Lord"?
Later, when I am older.
Later, when I have enjoyed life.
Later, when the relationship is secure.
Later, when I have enough money.
Later, when I am ready to stop.
Later.
And sometimes "later" becomes the word we use to keep God outside the rooms of our lives that we refuse to surrender.
But here is something we desperately need to understand.
Sin does not merely take us somewhere God told us not to go. It teaches us to love what is taking us away from Him.
That is why repentance is more than feeling bad after getting caught.
It is a turning of the heart.
It is the moment we stop defending what God has exposed.
It is when we stop calling bondage freedom.
It is when we stop asking God to make our idols comfortable.
It is when we finally admit:
"Lord, I have been giving away pieces of my life to things that cannot save me."
And that confession may hurt.
Because sometimes the truth of God reaches places we have spent years trying to keep hidden.
The secret habit.
The bitterness.
The envy.
The dishonesty.
The hidden compromise.
The relationship that has become more important than obedience.
The pride that refuses correction.
The spiritual performance that looks impressive to everyone except the God who sees the heart.
But conviction is not the same thing as hopeless condemnation.
God exposes sin because sin is deadly.
And the God who speaks truth about our condition is not powerless to rescue us from it.
There is something astonishing in the larger story of Ezekiel 16.
After describing Jerusalem's unfaithfulness and announcing the seriousness of His judgment, God speaks about covenant remembrance.
Ezekiel 16:60 says:
“Nevertheless I will remember my covenant with thee in the days of thy youth, and I will establish unto thee an everlasting covenant.” (KJV)
Nevertheless.
What a word.
After the exposure.
After the betrayal.
After the shame.
After the judgment.
Nevertheless.
God does not pretend that Jerusalem's sin was harmless.
He does not dismiss the evil.
He does not erase the need for justice.
Yet He declares that His covenant purposes have not been exhausted by His people's unfaithfulness.
And the chapter ends with a remarkable promise.
Ezekiel 16:63 speaks of the people remembering, being ashamed, and no longer opening their mouths in pride when God makes atonement for what they have done.
The Hebrew verb כַּפְּרִי (kapperi), from the root k-p-r, belongs to the biblical language of making atonement.
That matters.
Because the answer to sin is not simply pretending it never happened.
The answer requires God's merciful action to deal with guilt.
And when we read this passage in the light of the whole biblical story, we begin to see why the Gospel of Jesus Christ is such extraordinary news.
Ezekiel's immediate prophecy concerns Jerusalem, her covenant betrayal, judgment, and God's promised restoration.
But the wider Scriptures reveal the ultimate answer to humanity's sin in Jesus Christ.
The faithful Son of God came into a world of unfaithful sinners.
He did not come because humanity had finally become worthy of salvation.
He came because we needed a Savior.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired everything.
Not after we achieved spiritual perfection.
Not after we convinced everyone that we had changed.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
And this is where the story becomes almost unbearable in its beauty.
In Ezekiel, God exposes a people who spent His gifts pursuing false lovers.
At Calvary, we behold the Savior who gave Himself to redeem sinners who could never purchase their own salvation.
Do not misunderstand that comparison.
Jesus did not pay our idols to love us.
He did not negotiate with sin.
He did not make peace with evil.
He gave Himself as the sacrifice for sin, satisfying the demands of divine justice and opening the way for guilty people to be reconciled to God.
First Peter 3:18 says:
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God...” (KJV)
The just for the unjust.
The innocent for the guilty.
The faithful Savior for unfaithful sinners.
And suddenly, the scandal of Ezekiel 16 points us toward a question that every human heart must eventually answer.
If Jesus Christ gave Himself to bring us back to God, why do we keep running toward things that cannot save us?
Why do we cling to the chains He calls us to leave behind?
Why do we treat repentance as a punishment when it is the doorway back to fellowship with the One who loves us?
Why do we imagine that surrendering to Christ means losing everything, when He alone can give us the life we were created to live?
Perhaps because we have misunderstood grace.
We have mistaken grace for permission to remain unchanged.
But biblical grace does not merely forgive the sinner.
It also teaches the redeemed to turn away from ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 says:

“For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world.” (KJV)
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
Grace confronts what is destroying us.
Grace does not say, "Your sin does not matter."
Grace says, "Your sin is so serious that Christ died to save you from it, and His mercy is greater than your ability to rescue yourself."
And if you are reading this with a heavy heart because something in these words has exposed your own life, please hear what Scripture actually promises.
You are not required to pretend that you have never sinned.
You are called to confess your sin and turn to the Savior.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Those are not empty religious words.
They describe the mercy of God toward those who come to Him through Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have spent years trying to look like a Christian while privately struggling with something you are ashamed to name.
Maybe you once loved reading Scripture, but now your Bible stays closed for days.
Maybe prayer has become something you do only when life falls apart.
Maybe you have built a life that looks successful from the outside but feels spiritually empty on the inside.
Maybe you are exhausted from trying to serve two masters.
Or maybe you have wandered so far that you wonder whether returning is even possible.
Listen.
The answer is not to become better at hiding.
The answer is to come into the light.
Jesus said in John 6:37:
“...him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (KJV)
That is not a promise that sin is acceptable.
It is a promise that those who come to Christ will not find Him unwilling to receive them.
You do not have to make peace with the sin that is destroying you.
You do not have to keep financing the habits that are draining your soul.
You do not have to keep sacrificing your convictions to maintain the approval of people who cannot save you.
You can repent.
You can confess.
You can seek help.
You can begin walking in obedience, even when the first steps are difficult.
And when you stumble, you do not have to pretend you never fell.
You return to Christ in repentance and faith.
Because your hope is not in the perfection of your performance.
Your hope is in the perfection of your Savior.
This is what makes the Gospel so different from mere religious self-improvement.
Religion without grace can leave people trying desperately to earn acceptance.
But the Gospel announces salvation by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by our own works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And that same grace produces a changed life, created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10).
We do not obey so that Christ will finally decide to love us.
We obey because the Savior who loved us has redeemed us and called us to follow Him.
And that changes everything.
It changes how we see money.
It changes how we see relationships.
It changes how we see success.
It changes how we see our bodies, our words, our choices, and our future.
It changes what we are willing to sacrifice.
It changes whom we are willing to disappoint.
It changes what we do when nobody is watching.
And perhaps most importantly, it changes how we respond when God's Word confronts us.
Instead of asking, "How can I justify this?"
We begin asking, "Lord, how can I honor You?"
Instead of asking, "How close can I get to sin without consequences?"
We begin asking, "How closely can I walk with Jesus?"
Instead of asking, "What will I lose if I obey?"
We begin asking, "What is worth more than knowing Christ?"
That is the transformation the Gospel produces.
Not instant sinless perfection.
But a real and growing life of repentance, faith, obedience, and dependence upon the Holy Spirit.
And there is one more thing we must not miss.
The Bible does not end with the people of God forever pictured as an unfaithful wife.
In Revelation 19:7, the redeemed are pictured in the language of a bride prepared for the Lamb.
And Ephesians 5:25 declares:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” (KJV)
The One who loved the Church gave Himself for her.
The One who calls His people to holiness is the One who sacrificed Himself to redeem them.
The One who exposes our sin is also the One through whom forgiveness and cleansing are offered.
This is the glory of Christ.
He does not merely improve our public image.
He changes our standing before God and begins transforming our hearts.
He does not simply teach us to manage our shame.
He brings us into the light of His truth and mercy.
He does not tell us to build a convincing religious performance.
He calls us to follow Him.
And if this truth is reaching somewhere deep inside you, do not rush past it.
What am I still paying for with my peace, my time, my obedience, or my devotion that is quietly pulling me away from Jesus?
You may already know the answer.
And if you do, this is a moment to respond.
Not to perform repentance for an audience.
But to be honest before God.
And if God has already begun restoring something in your life, consider sharing your testimony. Someone else may need to know that repentance and restoration are possible through Jesus Christ.
You do not have to disclose private details to strangers. God sees what others cannot, and sincere repentance does not depend upon a public comment.
But there is something beautiful about believers encouraging one another to keep looking toward Christ.
And please do not let this message end with you.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a person who looks completely fine but is spiritually exhausted.
Someone who has been quietly drifting.
Someone who still believes in God but has stopped seeking Him.
Someone who has mistaken success for peace.
Someone who feels too ashamed to return.
Not merely because it may reach more people, but because the truth of God's Word deserves to be heard beyond the walls of a church building.
Not as another piece of content to forget, but as a reminder to revisit Ezekiel 16, examine your heart, and remember the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.
Believers need more than an occasional emotional moment.
We need Scripture.
We need prayer.
We need correction.
We need encouragement.
We need sound teaching.
We need a daily return to the truth that Jesus Christ is Lord.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a personality around religious content.
Not to replace the local church or the fellowship and accountability believers need.

But to help bring Scripture-centered encouragement, biblical discipleship, Gospel truth, and spiritual nourishment to people who might otherwise never stop long enough to consider the condition of their souls.
Those resources are intended to help people study the Bible, strengthen their understanding of the faith, and develop a deeper relationship with the Lord.
And there is another way you can participate in this mission.
It is a voluntary act of generosity that helps support the continuing work of creating, maintaining, and expanding this ministry's resources and Gospel-centered outreach.
For believers who regard their giving as an expression of worship, such support can be part of their broader stewardship and generosity before God.
Scripture teaches us to give willingly, not under pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
That is the spirit in which this invitation is offered.
You do not earn forgiveness by donating.
You do not become more loved by Jesus because you contribute financially.
Salvation is God's gift. Supporting Gospel ministry is a voluntary response of gratitude, love, and conviction.
Your contribution can help sustain the effort behind the articles, the teaching, the resources, and the outreach.
These products can serve as reminders of faith, opportunities to share biblical encouragement, and gifts for people you love.
The Gospel itself is never for sale.
The mercy of Jesus Christ cannot be purchased.
And the invitation to repent, believe, and follow Him remains freely proclaimed.
Before you leave, I want to return to the image that began this entire story.
An abandoned child.
Helpless.
Unwanted.
Unable to save herself.
And the Lord passing by.
"Live."
Then the child grows.
Receives blessings.
Forgets the Giver.
Turns toward false lovers.
Spends what she was given pursuing what cannot save.
And the God who had shown such mercy exposes the betrayal.
It is a painful story.
But the biblical story of redemption does not end with humanity's unfaithfulness.
It leads us to Jesus Christ.
The Savior who died for sinners.
The Savior who rose from the dead.
The Savior who calls people to repentance.
The Savior who forgives, cleanses, restores, and transforms those who come to Him in faith.
Maybe that is what you needed to remember today.
Not that your sin was small.
But that Christ is a great Savior.
Not that your wandering was harmless.
But that returning to Him is still the right response.
Not that your past can be rewritten as though it never happened.
But that your past does not have to remain the master of your future.
Because through Jesus Christ, guilt can be forgiven.
The enslaved can be set free.
The proud can be humbled.
The broken can find hope.
And sinners can become new creations in Christ.
So tonight, or wherever you are when these words reach you, consider praying with an honest heart:

"Lord Jesus, I have given my attention, affection, and devotion to things that cannot save me. I have sometimes loved Your gifts more than I have loved You. Forgive me for my sins. Teach me to turn away from everything that competes with my obedience to You. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Help me trust in You, walk in Your truth, and live a life that brings glory to Your name. I cannot save myself. My hope is in Your mercy. Amen."
And if you have reached the end of this article, I would love to ask you one final question.
What is one thing God has been teaching you to surrender so that you can follow Jesus more faithfully?
Because sometimes the testimony that helps another person is not "I have never fallen."
It is "Christ is still teaching me to walk."
There may be a person who has spent years believing that the only story their life can ever tell is the story of their failure.
Let them hear about the Savior who offers forgiveness and new life.
Let them know that sin does not have to have the final word.
Let them know that Jesus Christ is still calling sinners to repentance and faith.
You may have spent years giving your heart to things that could never save you—but Jesus gave His life to bring sinners back to God.
